cards.text: Paul the apostle is writing to the church in Corinth, and he's in the middle of a tough talk with them. He says, "I repeat: Let no one take me for a fool." But if they do, then fine, receive him as a fool, so he too may boast a little.

cards.question: Paul's about to boast about himself. True or false: Paul says this confident boasting is the way the Lord would speak.
Paul admits boasting is fool talk. So why does Paul decide to boast at all?

cards.text: Then Paul tells the church they gladly put up with fools, "since you are so wise." I think that compliment comes with a pinch in it, friend. Like when the boss says "bold choice" and walks away slowly.

cards.question: Paul lists what the Corinthians put up with from the boasters. True or false: Paul says they even put up with someone who strikes them in the face.

cards.text: Then Paul says, "To my shame I concede that we were too weak for that!" Friend, that's the most backwards apology I've ever heard. "I'm SO sorry I never pushed you around."

cards.question: Speaking as a fool, Paul says he can ___ what anyone else dares to boast about.

cards.text: And here comes the matching. Are they Hebrews? So is Paul. Are they Israelites? So is Paul. Every brag they've got, he's got a "me too" ready to go.

cards.question: One more "so am I" from Paul. The boasters claim to be descendants of someone, and Paul says he is too. Who?

cards.text: Paul's still matching the boasters one claim at a time. Are they servants of Christ? Then he adds, "I am speaking as if I were out of my mind."

cards.question: True or false: Paul says that as a servant of Christ, he's only about equal to the boasters.

cards.text: He's so much more, Paul says: in harder labor, in more imprisonments, in worse beatings, in frequent danger of death. Most people's brag list is promotions. Paul's brag list is BEATINGS.

cards.question: Paul gets specific about those beatings. Five times he received the same punishment from the Jews. What was it?

cards.text: Three times beaten with rods. Once stoned. Three times shipwrecked. And he spent a night and a day in the open sea. A night AND a day! Friend, I used to complain about the junk drawer. At least the junk drawer was DRY.

cards.question: On his many journeys, Paul faced danger from rivers, bandits and more. True or false: that includes danger from his own countrymen.
And it's not just danger for Paul. Along with labor and toil, what does Paul say he often went without?
All of that is trouble from the outside. What pressure does Paul say he faces daily?

cards.text: Then Paul asks, "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief?" Every church is a batch in this man's oven, and he's checking on every single one.

cards.question: If Paul must boast, he says he will boast of the things that show his ___.
Paul brings God into it. True or false: Paul says the God and Father of the Lord Jesus knows he is not lying.

cards.text: Then Paul tells one more story. In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest him. The whole city, locked down for ONE guy.

cards.question: Damascus is secured and the governor wants Paul arrested. How does Paul escape?

answers.text: Lowered in a basket through a window
Slipped out through the city gate

cards.text: Through a window in the wall, down in a basket, and he escaped the governor's grasp. The great apostle Paul. In a BASKET. And that's the story he tells while he's boasting. I LOVE this man.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 9 quotes "so am I", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The passage starts mid-argument ('I repeat'), but the opening card only calls it 'a tough talk.' It never says what Paul is repeating or that others in Corinth are boasting about themselves and comparing themselves to him. The baker meets 'boasting' with no idea why it matters or who 'they' are in the cards that follow.

rule.text: It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: 'Thirty days in chains' is a wrong answer to a which-thing question (which punishment), but it isn't a real detail from anywhere in the Bible. It was made up.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

findings.problem: The story card has 7 sentences. It also packs four separate moments into one card: beaten with rods, stoned, shipwrecked, and a night and a day in the open sea, plus the junk-drawer joke.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.
Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke blends the comparison into the Bible setting by putting an oven in Paul's world ('Every church is a batch in this man's oven'). Its action, checking on every batch, also matches the daily concern for the churches in 11:28, not 11:29. Verse 29 is about Paul being weak with the weak and burning with grief when someone is led into sin.

rule.text: 2. The everyday comparison must have the same action. 3. One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: King Aretas shows up for the first time, and the card never says who he is. The governor is identified only as 'under King Aretas.'

rule.text: The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."
